title: Lecture 4. Design by Contract: Assertions and Program Correctness
summary: This lecture introduces Design by Contract (DbC) methodology as a systematic approach to building reliable software. Students will learn to specify software behavior using preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants, understand how contracts guarantee program correctness, and apply assertion-based reasoning to ensure software quality. The lecture emphasizes practical application of DbC principles in object-oriented programming and their role in achieving program reliability.
learningObjectives: Understand the fundamental principles and philosophy of Design by Contract
Write and apply preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants to specify software behavior
Use assertions for runtime monitoring and debugging
Apply contract inheritance rules and understand behavioral subtyping
Evaluate how contracts contribute to program reliability and correctness
Integrate DbC techniques into object-oriented software construction practices

sections.title: Introduction to Design by Contract
learningGoals: Understand the motivation for formal contracts in software
Grasp the philosophical foundation of DbC
Recognize the relationship between contracts and program correctness

subsections.title: The Software Reliability Challenge
keyPoints: Software defects cost billions annually and can cause catastrophic failures
Traditional testing catches errors but cannot prove correctness
Need for systematic methods to specify and verify software behavior
DbC provides a bridge between informal specifications and formal verification
examples: Ariane 5 rocket failure due to contract violation (overflow)
Medical device failures from unspecified preconditions
Financial system errors from missing postconditions
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing evolution from ad-hoc testing to formal methods, highlighting DbC's position

subsections.title: The Contract Metaphor
keyPoints: Contracts as agreements between software components (client and supplier)
Each party has obligations and benefits
Client obligation: satisfy precondition; Benefit: postcondition guaranteed
Supplier obligation: establish postcondition; Benefit: assume precondition
Contracts make implicit assumptions explicit and verifiable
examples: Real-world contract: hiring a contractor to build a house
Software contract: sqrt function requires non-negative input
Library checkout system with borrowing rules
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Two-party contract diagram showing obligations and benefits for client and supplier

subsections.title: DbC Principles and Benefits
keyPoints: Principle 1: Separate concerns (what vs. how)
Principle 2: Make contracts explicit and checkable
Principle 3: Fail fast when contracts are violated
Benefits: documentation, debugging, testing, reliability, reusability
DbC as a design methodology, not just an implementation technique
examples: Self-documenting code through contracts
Automatic test oracle generation from postconditions
Contract-based component composition
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Mind map showing DbC principles and their benefits radiating outward

exercises: Identify implicit contracts in existing code snippets
Discuss scenarios where contracts would have prevented real-world software failures
Compare DbC with defensive programming approaches

sections.title: Preconditions: Specifying Client Obligations
learningGoals: Define and write effective preconditions
Understand when and how to check preconditions
Apply preconditions to prevent invalid operations

subsections.title: What Are Preconditions?
keyPoints: Preconditions define the valid states for calling a routine
Express constraints on arguments and object state
Client responsibility: ensure precondition before calling
Supplier right: assume precondition holds (no defensive checks needed)
Syntax: require clause in Eiffel, @requires in JML, assert at method start
examples: Stack.pop requires not stack.is_empty
Array access requires valid index: 0 <= i < array.length
Bank withdrawal requires balance >= amount and amount > 0
File operations require file.is_open
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flowchart showing precondition check before method execution

subsections.title: Writing Effective Preconditions
keyPoints: Be precise: use boolean expressions, not natural language
Be complete: cover all necessary conditions
Be minimal: don't over-specify (allow maximum flexibility)
Use pure expressions: no side effects in contract clauses
Consider both argument validity and object state
examples: Good: require x > 0 and y > 0
Bad: require x is positive (ambiguous)
Over-specified: require x == 5 (too restrictive when x > 0 suffices)
Side-effect error: require list.remove(item) (modifies state)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code comparison showing weak vs. strong preconditions with examples

subsections.title: Precondition Violations and Error Handling
keyPoints: Precondition violation indicates client error (bug in caller)
Should not be caught and handled (unlike exceptions)
Fail fast: detect violations as early as possible
Runtime monitoring: enable during development, optionally disable in production
Clear error messages help identify the faulty caller
examples: Assertion failure with stack trace pointing to caller
Precondition violation in sqrt(-1) caught during testing
Production deployment strategies: monitoring levels
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing precondition violation detection and program termination

exercises: Write preconditions for common data structure operations (insert, delete, search)
Identify missing preconditions in buggy code examples
Debate: Should preconditions be checked in production code?

sections.title: Postconditions: Guaranteeing Results
learningGoals: Define and write comprehensive postconditions
Use postconditions to specify method behavior
Understand the relationship between postconditions and correctness

subsections.title: Postcondition Fundamentals
keyPoints: Postconditions specify what must be true after routine execution
Express guarantees about return values and state changes
Supplier responsibility: establish postcondition
Client benefit: rely on postcondition without inspecting implementation
Syntax: ensure clause in Eiffel, @ensures in JML
examples: Stack.push(x) ensures not is_empty and top = x
List.sort ensures is_sorted and same_elements(old list)
Account.deposit(amount) ensures balance = old balance + amount
Search function ensures (result >= 0 implies array[result] = key) and (result = -1 implies key not in array)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Before/after state diagram showing postcondition satisfaction

subsections.title: The 'old' Keyword and State Comparison
keyPoints: 'old' refers to value at routine entry (pre-state)
Essential for specifying state changes
Captures snapshot of mutable objects
Enables relational postconditions (new vs. old state)
Implementation: runtime stores old values when monitoring enabled
examples: ensure balance = old balance + amount
ensure count = old count + 1
ensure list.has(item) and list.count = old list.count + 1
ensure array is permutation of old array
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing pre-state (old values) and post-state with postcondition verification

subsections.title: Complete Behavioral Specification
keyPoints: Postconditions should fully characterize routine behavior
Specify both positive effects (what changes) and frame conditions (what doesn't)
Handle all cases: normal execution and boundary conditions
Combine multiple clauses for complex specifications
Balance completeness with readability
examples: Binary search: ensures (found implies array[result] = key) and (not found implies key not in array)
Queue operations: enqueue/dequeue with count and element preservation
Sorting with stability: ensures is_sorted and preserves_relative_order
Graph algorithms: ensures path_exists implies path_found and path_is_shortest
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree showing different postcondition clauses for different execution paths

exercises: Write complete postconditions for sorting algorithms
Identify incomplete postconditions and add missing guarantees
Create postconditions that specify both functional and performance properties

sections.title: Class Invariants: Maintaining Object Consistency
learningGoals: Understand the role of class invariants in object-oriented design
Write invariants that capture object consistency constraints
Apply invariant preservation rules across all class methods

subsections.title: Class Invariant Concept
keyPoints: Invariant: property that must hold for all instances at all stable times
Stable time: before and after any public method call (not during execution)
Captures the consistency constraints of the class abstraction
Every public method must preserve the invariant
Constructor must establish the invariant
examples: BankAccount: invariant balance >= 0
Date: invariant 1 <= day <= days_in_month(month, year)
BinarySearchTree: invariant is_binary_search_tree
Stack: invariant (is_empty implies count = 0) and (count >= 0)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: State diagram showing invariant holding at stable points, potentially violated during method execution

subsections.title: Writing and Checking Invariants
keyPoints: Syntax: invariant clause in class definition
Should be pure boolean expressions over object state
Automatically checked after constructor and after each public method
Private methods may temporarily violate invariant
Invariant strengthens postcondition and weakens precondition of all methods
examples: Bounded queue: invariant 0 <= count <= capacity
Linked list: invariant count = actual_node_count
Circle: invariant radius > 0
Sorted collection: invariant is_sorted
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Class diagram with invariant clause and method contracts showing invariant integration

subsections.title: Invariants and Object-Oriented Design
keyPoints: Invariants define the valid states of an abstraction
Guide the design of constructors and methods
Help identify which operations are valid for a class
Invariants must be preserved by all public operations
Strong invariants lead to simpler method contracts
examples: Designing a bounded buffer with capacity invariant
Date class with complex day/month/year relationships
Graph class maintaining edge consistency
Cache with size and validity invariants
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram annotated with invariants and showing how they constrain method implementations

exercises: Write invariants for common data structures (queue, priority queue, hash table)
Identify invariant violations in buggy class implementations
Design a class where the invariant guides the choice of operations

sections.title: Assertion Monitoring and Debugging
learningGoals: Configure and use assertion monitoring effectively
Apply DbC for systematic debugging
Understand performance trade-offs of runtime checking

subsections.title: Runtime Assertion Checking
keyPoints: Assertions can be monitored at runtime for validation
Multiple monitoring levels: none, preconditions only, all contracts
Development: enable all checks for maximum safety
Production: selective checking based on performance requirements
Assertion violations indicate bugs, not exceptional conditions
examples: Eiffel assertion monitoring levels: no, require, ensure, invariant, all
Java assert statement with -ea flag
C assert macro with NDEBUG flag
Custom assertion frameworks with configurable levels
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Configuration matrix showing different assertion levels and when to use them

subsections.title: Contract-Based Debugging
keyPoints: Contracts pinpoint the exact location of bugs
Precondition violation: bug in caller
Postcondition violation: bug in callee implementation
Invariant violation: bug in class implementation
Systematic debugging: follow the contract trail
examples: Stack overflow detected by precondition on push
Sorting bug revealed by postcondition failure
Invariant violation after delete operation reveals corruption
Debugging workflow: violation → identify responsible party → fix
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Debugging flowchart using contract violations to locate bugs

subsections.title: Performance Considerations
keyPoints: Assertion checking has runtime cost (typically 5-30% overhead)
Cost varies by assertion complexity and frequency of calls
Strategies: disable in production, selective checking, sampling
Some critical contracts may be kept in production
Modern compilers can optimize some assertions away
examples: Expensive invariant: is_sorted on large collections
Cheap precondition: x != null
Production strategy: keep preconditions, disable postconditions
Critical systems: keep all checks despite performance cost
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Performance graph showing overhead vs. assertion level with deployment recommendations

exercises: Configure assertion monitoring for a sample project
Use contract violations to debug intentionally buggy code
Measure and analyze performance impact of different assertion levels

sections.title: Contract Inheritance and Behavioral Subtyping
learningGoals: Understand how contracts interact with inheritance
Apply the Liskov Substitution Principle through contracts
Write correct contracts in inheritance hierarchies

subsections.title: The Liskov Substitution Principle
keyPoints: LSP: subtype objects must be substitutable for supertype objects
Behavioral compatibility, not just structural compatibility
Contracts formalize behavioral subtyping requirements
Subtype must honor supertype's contract with clients
Foundation for polymorphism and safe code reuse
examples: Rectangle/Square problem: violates LSP without proper contracts
Bird/Penguin hierarchy: flying behavior
Collection hierarchy: different performance guarantees
Payment method hierarchy with different validation rules
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Class hierarchy showing LSP violation and correction through contracts

subsections.title: Contract Inheritance Rules
keyPoints: Precondition rule: may only weaken (or-logic with parent)
Postcondition rule: may only strengthen (and-logic with parent)
Invariant rule: may only strengthen (and-logic with parent)
Rationale: preserve substitutability and client expectations
Formal: subtype contract ⊆ supertype contract
examples: Weakening precondition: PositiveInteger.set(x) requires x > 0, Integer.set(x) requires x >= 0 (invalid!)
Strengthening postcondition: SortedList.add ensures is_sorted (valid)
Invariant strengthening: BoundedStack adds capacity constraint
Valid override: relaxing input constraints, tightening output guarantees
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Contract lattice showing valid and invalid contract refinements in inheritance

subsections.title: Practical Contract Inheritance
keyPoints: Use 'require else' for precondition weakening
Use 'ensure then' for postcondition strengthening
Inherited invariants automatically conjoined
Check contract compatibility during design
Tool support for verifying contract inheritance rules
examples: Shape hierarchy with area calculation contracts
File system hierarchy: ReadOnlyFile vs. WritableFile
Collection hierarchy: List, Set, Bag with different contracts
Account hierarchy: CheckingAccount, SavingsAccount with different rules
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code example showing proper contract inheritance syntax and semantics

exercises: Identify LSP violations in class hierarchies and fix with contracts
Design a class hierarchy with proper contract inheritance
Analyze real-world framework hierarchies for contract compliance

subsections.title: Limitations and Complementary Techniques

Some properties are undecidable or too complex to specify
DbC complements, not replaces, testing and other verification
Need for integration with type systems, static analysis, formal methods
Practical adoption challenges: learning curve, tool support, legacy code

Combining DbC with unit testing for comprehensive validation
